spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad, representing all encounters between one player and one referee
the primary analysis includes N=99,645 dyads
there are 1,214 unique players (1,015 light-skinned, 199 dark-skinned)
there are 2,768 unique referees
there are 1,241 total red card events across all dyads
two independent raters coded player skin tone from photographs on a 5-point scale (0=very light to 1=very dark)
inter-rater correlation was r=0.923, described as excellent reliability
light skin was defined as an average rating ≤0.25 (n=83,655 dyads)
dark skin was defined as an average rating ≥0.75 (n=15,990 dyads)
medium skin tone (0.25-0.75) was excluded from the primary comparison to give the clearest contrast
the binary outcome was defined as any red card received in the dyad (1=yes, 0=no)
red cards are rare: 1.2% of light-skinned dyads and 1.4% of dark-skinned dyads received one
player position (11 categories) was included as a covariate
league country (4 categories) was included as a covariate
log(games), the natural log of games played in the dyad, was included as an exposure-adjustment covariate

spans.note: rationale explaining why position, league, and games were chosen as covariates

spans.assertion: 21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone (players without photos)
7,471 dyads were excluded for missing position
732 dyads were excluded for missing height/weight, for a complete case analysis
17,015 dyads with medium skin tone were excluded from the primary analysis
the final analytic sample size is 99,645 dyads
logistic regression was used as the model
the model formula was specified as logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(dark_skin) + β2(position) + β3(league) + β4(log_games)
the average marginal effect (AME) of dark_skin was used as the primary estimand, representing the adjusted risk difference
the exponentiated coefficient of dark_skin was used as the secondary estimand, representing the adjusted odds ratio
standard errors were clustered at the player level (each player appears in ~82 dyads on average)
a log transformation was used for games because the relationship between games and red-card probability is non-linear with diminishing marginal effect
Model 2 was tested, adding height and weight as covariates
Model 3 was tested, adding yellow cards as a proxy for aggressive play style
Model 4 was tested, changing clustering from the player level to the referee level
Model 5 was tested, using continuous skin tone (0-1) instead of the binary dark/light split
Model 1 (primary): risk difference 0.258pp, 95% CI [0.001, 0.515], p=0.049
Model 2 (+height/weight): risk difference 0.237pp, 95% CI [-0.017, 0.491], p=0.068, marked non-significant
Model 3 (+yellow cards): risk difference 0.264pp, 95% CI [0.008, 0.520], p=0.043
Model 5 (continuous skin tone): risk difference 0.229pp, p=0.028
the result becomes non-significant (p=0.068) when height and weight are added, suggesting the finding is not robust to all reasonable covariate choices
with player-level clustering (primary), OR=1.222, 95% CI [1.012, 1.475], p=0.037
with referee-level clustering, OR=1.222, 95% CI [1.043, 1.432], p=0.013
clustering by referee yields a more significant p-value but does not address the other concerns with the finding
a likelihood ratio test for the dark_skin × league interaction gave LR=23.0, p<0.001
this highly significant interaction indicates the effect varies substantially across leagues
in England the log-odds coefficient is +0.403 (dark>light), p=0.010
in Germany the log-odds coefficient is +0.716 (dark>light)
in France the log-odds coefficient is -0.282 (light>dark)
in Spain the log-odds coefficient is -0.007, essentially no difference
